https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-steps-up-m.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Mtih Ukrainian trains are increasingly the target of Russian drones Image: Ukrainian State Emergency Service/AFP Advertisement Recent months have seen a rise in Russian drone attacks on locomotives, stations, and infrastructure. More than 1,600 attacks were reported in the first eight months of 2026, according to Oleh Holovashchenko from Ukrzaliznytsia, the state rail operator. On September 16, a train traveling between the capital Kyiv and Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine was struck by a Russian drone. The day before, another train in the Volhynia region was attacked near the Polish border. Two days earlier, a drone had struck the locomotive of a passenger train at the Yahodyn border crossing, just two kilometers (1.2 miles) from Polish territory. Nobody was injured, as Ukrzaliznytsia's monitoring system had previously detected the drone and the train had been evacuated about 15 minutes before the attack. At the time, CIA Director David Petraeus was on another train at the same station. A separate train carrying several former European leaders, including ex-British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and security advisers had stopped at the station earlier the same day. The Ukrainian authorities believe that this diplomatic train was the drone's actual target, but the train departed earlier than scheduled. 'Putin's terror' against Ukrainian logistics Russia has damaged or destroyed more than 500 Ukrainian locomotives since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. More than half of these attacks happened this year, according to a post on the social media platform X by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. He said that part of "Putin's terror" was to destabilize Ukraine's logistics system. The minister called on international partners to tighten sanctions against Russia further and to provide financial assistance to the Ukrainian government so that it can procure more locomotives that are compatible with Ukraine's Soviet-era broad-gauge (1,520 millimeters or almost 5 feet). "Ukraine's railway keeps the country moving," Sybiha said. "It enables the rapid evacuation of civilians from frontline areas, transports essential cargo, and keeps grain and other critical goods moving across the country." Russia was specifically targeting locomotives because they were ideal from a technical point of view, said Vasyl Shevchenko, a former Ukrainian deputy transport minister. "A locomotive's thermal signature is very large, and almost impossible to miss," he told DW. "The impact of a strike can be devastating, because 50 kilograms (110 pounds) of explosives in a diesel locomotive can cause several metric tons of fuel to detonate and completely destroy it. A strike on an electric locomotive will cause a fire that can paralyze an entire stretch of track. That's why they are targeting areas where the loss of a single train can bring traffic to a standstill." Shevchenko also pointed out that locomotives could not be replaced immediately but had to be ordered in advance and this could take years. Ukrzaliznytsia says that negotiations are underway with various international partners and a contract has already been signed with the French company Alstom. These locomotives are scheduled to start arriving next year. In the meantime, trains are also being repaired. "While our top priorities used to be saving on costs, providing comfort to the train crew and making sure the trains were attractive, these have changed," Holovashchenko said. "What is most important today is that the locomotive is technically sound and ready to transport passengers and freight." But he added that it was difficult to protect trains against Russia's weapons. Ukrainian authorities are trying to ensure trains are evacuated before a drone strikes Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS Zelenskyy intensifies protection of critical infrastructure On September 15, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a meeting of the staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief to discuss strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure and logistics. The key issues were contracts for the production of protection systems for critical infrastructure and logistics, but he added that there were plans to expand the electronic warfare component and reorganize the operation of designated mobile fire teams, as well as strengthening air defense lines. Zelenskyy said that decisions on backup logistics routes in frontline regions were also being made, and he had instructed Ukraine's Finance Ministry of to find additional funding for the logistics sector. Experts say it is technically very easy to target a locomotive Image: Odesa Regional Military Administration/AFP Ukrzaliznytsia sets up monitoring centers According to Holovashchenko, Ukrzaliznytsia is also seeking its own answers to the new challenges and there are plans to develop early detection systems. He said that a monitoring center had been established to track the movement of drones and trains all over Ukraine. The fact that Russia has started to use jet-powered Shahed-type drones , which are much faster than previous models, has made it more difficult and given less time to respond. "We used to wait longer to stop trains so we could evacuate passengers," Holovashchenko said. "Now, there are more precautionary stops. But in general, we try not to go into areas where there is a potential danger." Buses are deployed in areas of particularly high risk and the "train plus bus" concept is being expanded in cooperation with military authorities. Passengers are also being given instructions on how to respond in the event of an alarm and advised to try to get further away from a station than previously. The most difficult question remains where they should be evacuated to. Holovashchenko said that the monitoring centers had access to maps showing all the shelters along train routes and that dispatchers always tried to stop trains near them, but this was not always possible. He said that train personnel were receiving special psychological support to help passengers. Ukrzaliznytsia is currently preparing for winter, while working with foundations and other donors to ensure that trains will be heated. Evacuations will be even more difficult as temperatures drop. "This is no easy task. We're providing blankets, rain jackets, and equipment so that train staff can supply passengers with at least the bare necessities if their train comes to a standstill in the middle of nowhere because of a snowstorm, Holovashchenko said. This article was originally published in Ukrainian. (Image credit: Eugene Nekrasov via Getty Images) Copy link Facebook X Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Share this article 1 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter If your blond preteen seems to be turning into a brunette, you're not imagining things. For some children, hair that starts out platinum blond gradually becomes darker and may end up dark brown, or even black, as they grow. So what causes this change? The short answer is that hair color is controlled by a complex interplay of genes, pigment-producing cells and, later in childhood, hormones. Scientists understand many of the genes involved in hair color , but they are still trying to find out why some blond children's hair darkens while others' locks remain blond for life. Latest Videos From Live Science Watch full video here: "It depends on their genetic inheritance," Desmond Tobin , a professor of dermatological science at University College Dublin, told Live Science in an email. Hair gets its color from a pigment called melanin, which is produced by specialized cells called melanocytes in hair follicles. There are two main types of melanin: eumelanin, which produces brown and black shades , and pheomelanin, which contributes yellow and red tones to hair. The amount and type of melanin produced by a follicle largely determine the color of the hair that grows from it. You may like Are redheads going extinct? A man's sudden fainting episodes landed him in the hospital — and a hair dye was to blame Aging doesn't look the same for everyone at the molecular level — it's 'individualized and context-dependent' Sign up for our newsletter Sign up for our weekly Life's Little Mysteries newsletter to get the latest mysteries before they appear online. In general, more eumelanin means darker hair . For example, during pregnancy, high levels of estrogen and progesterone can encourage hair darkening as more eumelanin is produced. The activity of hair follicles isn't necessarily fixed throughout childhood. As children grow, the biological signals controlling pigment production can change, too. From blond to brown For many blond children, the most noticeable darkening happens around puberty, typically between about 10 and 13 years old, Tobin said. It is likely the hormonal changes during puberty , such as estrogens and androgens that stimulate an increased production of eumelanin, that gradually turn blond hair darker over time, he said. "Those that remain blond typically have a genetically determined reduction in eumelanin pigment formation," Tobin added. Exactly how hormones might cause this change, however, is still something of a mystery. What to read next 1 million people's genes reveal the heritability of the Big Five personality traits — and it's complicated Cells from your mother likely infiltrated your brain in the womb, and they could survive for decades, study reveals We remember little to nothing of early childhood — and a recent mouse study may help explain why The most noticeable hair darkening seems to happen around puberty. (Image credit: Halfpoint Images via Getty Images) One clue comes from a group of hormones called melanocortins. One of these, alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), is involved in telling pigment-producing cells to make more melanin. In our skin, alpha-MSH is triggered by ultraviolet (UV) light . UV light can damage DNA in skin cells that, via a cellular signaling pathway, encourages the release of alpha-MSH to make the skin tan. But in hair, things get, well, hairy. Scientists haven't shown that a rise in alpha-MSH, testosterone, estrogen or any particular hormone is what makes blond hair darken. The melanocortin system shows that hormones can tell pigment-producing cells to make more eumelanin. What remains unclear is whether changes in this system are actually responsible for blond hair darkening during puberty. "We haven't yet identified the genes that control this process," Wojciech Branicki , a researcher who studies the genetics of human pigmentation at Jagiellonian University in Poland, told Live Science in an email. Related mysteries Why do we grow more hair on our heads than on our bodies? How fast does hair grow? Why do we lose so much hair? One possibility Branicki suggested is that hormones may affect children's hair follicles differently depending on their genetic background. For now, researchers don't know which genes are involved or how they interact with hormonal changes during puberty, as more research is needed. Branicki posits that in some children, the hormones could induce the production of melanin or the transport of pigment within the hair follicle. In other words, two children could start out with similarly blond hair but respond differently to the hormonal changes as their bodies develop. One might continue producing relatively little eumelanin and stay blond, while the other's follicles might gradually ramp up pigment production, causing new batches of hair to grow darker. "Research on human genome variation is quite advanced, but not all aspects have been explained yet," Branicki said. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition looks to be coming to an end. Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition looks to be coming to an end. Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty Images First Edition newsletter Israel Friday briefing: Israel has a dilemma - can its opposition govern with Palestinian parties? In today’s newsletter: Benjamin Netanyahu has been left without a majority, now it is up to the coalition to find out whether the desire for change will prove to be a defining political moment Libby Brooks Fri 30 Oct 2026 02.44 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 02.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. It was described by many Israelis as the most consequential election in their country’s history. And, as the final votes were tallied, it has delivered a result that presents Israel with a significant dilemma. Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition has lost its mandate while the opposition has a clear majority: but only if the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, led by retired general Gadi Eisenkot, is prepared to make a governing pact with Palestinian Israeli parties, which have secured a historic result. But the country that is desperate for change remains bitterly divided. After a campaign mired in racism, during which Israel’s far-right demonised the Palestinian population as the enemy within, Netanyahu has gone further since Tuesday’s vote, claiming that Palestinian-led parties have “stolen the election”, despite Israeli authorities insisting there is no evidence of election fraud. As coalition talks commence, I spoke to our chief Middle East correspondent Emma Graham-Harrison in Tel Aviv, about false narratives and the stark choice facing the country. But first, the headlines. Five big stories UK politics | John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances. Patrick Stewart | The acclaimed British stage and screen actor renowned for both Shakespeare and sci-fi, died at his home in Los Angeles after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia”, his longtime spokesperson said. Environment | One of the most ambitious nature recovery projects ever undertaken in England can go ahead after campaigners announced they had raised £30m to buy an estate in Northumberland. Europe | Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday for at least 69 people who died in a high-speed rail collision , as hospitals continued to treat dozens of injured passengers and train drivers went on strike to urge more investment in railway safety. US news | The Trump administration has opened a criminal investigation in California over claims that thousands of noncitizens are registered to vote in the state, and has begun subpoenaing election officials. In depth: There is no evidence of election fraud View image in fullscreen Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, is committed to working with Jewish Israeli opposition parties. Photograph: Mahmoud Illean/AP With the final results released early on Friday local time, Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats, compared with 48 for the grouping led by rival Eisenkot. Palestinian parties won 19 seats, a record high. No single party has ever claimed a majority of 61 seats, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions. With neither bloc reaching the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, Israeli president Isaac Herzog is expected to invite the party most likely to be able to form a government to start coalition negotiations, and has already urged politicians to have an “open mind” before talks begin. The country potentially faces weeks of rancour and uncertainty. Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, told Israeli media on Thursday that he was meeting Eisenkot and others for initial talks. If the opposition can’t agree some kind of coalition, or even secure Palestinian support for a minority government, Netanyahu may have a lifeline. He is already pushing for a right-wing governing coalition, and would probably welcome new elections or a lengthy period of uncertainty during which he will stay on as caretaker prime minister. And yet throughout the campaign, voters’ discontent with Netanyahu was evident. That didn’t mean a shift to the left: young Israelis are more rightwing than older generations, as Emma wrote about here . The national conversation ahead of the election was dominated by security at home and abroad. Although he was in charge on 7 October 2023, when Hamas attacks resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians, the prime minister tried to shift blame on to the security services. His opponents pledged a state commission of inquiry into the events of 7 October, and spoke to voters’ concerns about the social toll of three years of multi-front wars, and anger about the draft exemption for ultra-orthodox young men when other Israelis are spending hundreds of days on reserve duty. Netanyahu’s false narrative Throughout the campaign, Netanyahu and his far-right allies have framed Palestinian voters – who make up about 20% of the population – as a direct threat to ​the state, with Netanyahu repeating the slogan “the right or Palestine”, which rhymes in Hebrew. “It’s both tragic and depressing,” Emma tells me, “attempting to paint Palestinians as untrustworthy citizens with dual loyalties, a racist trope that also appears in antisemitic attacks.” This tactic extended to election day, when voters received a robocall purporting to come from the prime minister falsely claiming that Palestinian party leaders had been caught with envelopes full of cash. Netanyahu and his allies repeatedly made claims about high turnout in Palestinian areas, in a bid to get his own voters out. Then on Wednesday night, Netanyahu reacted to the high Palestinian turnout and success of Arab Israeli parties by claiming, again without providing evidence, they had “stolen the election,” calling for the central elections committee and Shin Bet internal security agency to investigate foreign interference in the vote. These claims were amplified by far-right Israeli finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, who called for the arrest of Arab Israeli leaders. He was swiftly accused of using smear tactics to cling to power. Eisenkot warned that Likud and Netanyahu “have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election”. President Herzog stepped in with a rebuke to the prime minister and said “we must avoid tarnishing an entire community”. Meanwhile, Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson rejected “ridiculous and dangerous” accusations his country had interfered in Tuesday’s election. It bears repeating: Israeli police and the central elections committee have said there is no evidence of election fraud. The Palestinian-led parties who could be kingmakers There was a surge in support for Arab parties after Palestinian citizens came out in historic numbers to vote. Many had boycotted previous elections “on the grounds that participating endorses a discriminatory system or because they felt their representatives had little leverage”, Emma explains. But this year, the mood changed: “They’re watching ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, a genocidal war in Gaza, and are under huge pressure inside Israel from an openly racist government, which has allowed organised crime to soar, ramped up home demolitions, and targeted political speech. They felt that, if Netanyahu managed to get another mandate with his far right allies including [extremist security minister] Ben-Gvir, this would only accelerate.” The Joint List – which represents a number of mainly leftist Israeli Arab-led parties – is led by Yousef Jabareen. He has previously said the Joint ​List could not join an Eisenkot-led government because of its support for Israel’s ‌military operation in Gaza and southern Lebanon, but has left open the possibility of bolstering a minority government through confidence votes. The other main Palestinian party, Ra’am, is led by Mansour Abbas, and includes a Jewish former chief of police as number two on their slate, a signal of their commitment to working with Jewish Israelis but also their desire to tackle organised crime, which is a big issue for the Palestinian population. Ra’am joined Naftali Bennett’s government in 2021, the first time a Palestinian party entered an Israeli coalition, but their pact collapsed after 18 months, partly because of disagreements over the occupied West Bank. The big dilemma A survey taken as polls closed on Tuesday showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu. While Eisenkot has not ruled out cooperating with Palestinians because of their race, he has effectively barred them from a future coalition by laying out conditions for any partner which are politically impossible for them to accept. Still, Emma notes an inconsistency: Palestinian citizens play a key role in Israeli life, with outsized representation in professions from medics to security guards, including much of the team at Eisenkot’s election night HQ. “You would think some of these parties might ask, if you trust Palestinian citizens to secure your campaign events why don’t you trust them to be part of your government?” Emma points to a rarely referenced precedent from three decades ago, when Yitzhak Rabin relied on Palestinian support for a minority government as he sought a negotiated end to the Israel-Palestine conflict. Might such a compromise be possible now? “This whole campaign has been based on Israeli voters urgently wanting change, because Netanyahu has led them to the brink of disaster. And now they have voted, this is an existential moment,” she said “You have a parliamentary majority to bring about that change. Is your racism ultimately more important to you? What matters more: the desire to exclude Palestinians or the desire to get rid of Netanyahu?” What else we’ve been reading View image in fullscreen ‘It was like a youth club’ … Boogie Times Records in Romford. The Times leads with “Defence to benefit from off-the-book spending”, the Telegraph writes “Prepare for decade of pain, warn IFS”, and the i Paper leads on “No welfare cuts before election – as Britons face ‘worst decade’ for pay growth”, while the Mail has “Humiliation for Healey”. The Latest Photograph: The Guardian Shock and anger in Spain after deadly train crash Spain has begun three days of mourning after at least 69 people were killed and more than 100 were injured in a crash between two high-speed trains. The town of Urda has become the site of a major operation, as emergency services continue to search through the wreckage and relatives wait for news of their loved ones. There is growing public anger over the incident, which is the second fatal train collision in Spain in less than a year. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s Madrid correspondent, Sam Jones . Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings View image in fullscreen Illustration: Ben Jennings/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen An electric ferry in New York. Photograph: Climate Central Moving away from diesel-powered ferries to electric vessels has not been an easy task. Batteries are heavy, which means more power is needed to propel electric boats forward through significant resistance. But more companies are finding solutions to the problem and creating workable vessels that reduce emissions. One such company is Vessev, whose electric ferries rely on underwater wings called hydrofoils that lift the boat above the water. This dramatically reduces drag by up to 66%, making their boats more energy-efficient. Swedish company Candela are designing boats, they claim, which can reduce energy use by 80% compared with conventional vessels of a similar type. “I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Eric Laakmann, the chief executive and co-founder of Vessev, said.
